title: EPPS 6302 Methods of Data Collection
text:
About the Course
EPPS 6302 focuses on the foundations of empirical research and the decisions involved in producing credible data.
The course considers how research questions are translated into measurable concepts, how samples are selected, how data are gathered, and how the strengths and limitations of different collection methods affect the conclusions that can reasonably be drawn.
Topics may include survey design, interviews, sampling, measurement, reliability, validity, observational methods, and ethical considerations in social research.
As assignments are completed, this page will serve as an organized record of my work throughout the semester.

title: Assignment 5 – Government Data API
text:
In this assignment I used the GovInfo search interface to find recent documents related to the Foreign Relations Committee. :contentReferenceoaicite:1

I went to https://www.govinfo.gov/app/search/.
I searched for Foreign Relations Committee hearings and filtered the results to the most recent Congress.
From the search results page, I used the Download Results option to export the metadata as both CSV and JSON files.
I saved these files into my Quarto project under the data/ folder.
Using the provided govtdata01.R template, I modified the script so that it:

Reads the CSV and JSON files from the data/ folder,
Extracts the pdfLink for each result,
Downloads the 10 most recent PDFs into the files/ folder,
Pauses briefly between downloads to avoid overwhelming the server. :contentReferenceoaicite:2


After running the script, the ten PDFs appear under files/, and the _quarto.yml resources: setting ensures that they are copied into the rendered website.

title: Assignment 5 – Government Data API
text:
2. Difficulties encountered

2.1 Technical and practical issues
While scraping the government data, I ran into several practical difficulties:

File paths and working directory
The script assumes a specific working directory. If RStudio was not set to the project root, the read.csv() and read_json() calls failed with “cannot open file” errors. I fixed this by explicitly setting the working directory and using relative paths like data/... and files/....
CSV header rows and formats
The CSV export from GovInfo includes explanatory header lines before the actual field names. If I did not skip these rows, the data frame loaded incorrectly. Using skip = 2 (as in the template) made the import work reliably. :contentReferenceoaicite:3
Inconsistent or missing links
Not every record has a clean pdfLink. In some cases, the JSON had missing or NA values, so the code had to be careful about indexing and only trying to download valid URLs.
Download reliability and rate limiting
Downloading multiple PDFs in a row sometimes led to slow responses or temporary failures. The tryCatch() wrapper and a random Sys.sleep() between 1–3 seconds helped handle occasional errors gracefully and kept the script from appearing abusive to the server.



2.2 How usable is the scraped data?
The metadata and PDFs from GovInfo are quite usable, but not “analysis-ready”:

The JSON metadata provides structured fields such as titles, dates, and committee names, which are very helpful for filtering and organizing hearings.
However, the actual content of the hearings is embedded in PDF documents, which are not directly machine-readable. To analyze the text (for example, topic modeling or sentiment analysis), I would still need to run an additional PDF-to-text extraction step.
Some records are duplicated across different formats, and their identifiers are not always intuitive, so the user must carefully deduplicate or standardize IDs.

Overall, the scraped data works well for building a corpus of documents, but it requires extra preprocessing before any quantitative analysis.


2.3 How the process could be improved
Several improvements could make this workflow smoother and more robust:

Use relative paths and project options
Instead of hard-coding setwd("yourpath"), it would be better to rely on RStudio Projects or the here package so that the script always starts from the project root, regardless of machine or user.
Filter and validate links before download
Adding checks to ensure that pdfLink is not NA and that it starts with https:// would avoid wasted download attempts.
Automated logging of errors
Extending the tryCatch() block to write failed URLs and error messages to a log file would make it easier to re-run only the failed downloads later.
Text extraction and additional data cleaning
A next step would be to automatically convert the downloaded PDFs to text (using packages like pdftools) and store them as cleaned .txt files. This would make the data much more usable for statistical or text-mining analysis.
Parameterization
Turning the script into a function where I can pass the committee name, number of documents, and output folder as arguments would make it easier to reuse the code for other committees or topics.

title: Assignment 5 – Government Data API
text:
3. Summary
This assignment showed how to move from a search interface on a government website to a reproducible R script that downloads primary documents into a structured project. Setting up the file paths correctly, handling messy CSV/JSON exports, and dealing with download errors were the main challenges. Once those issues were resolved, the process of automatically pulling the ten most recent Foreign Relations Committee documents became straightforward, and I now have a reusable template for future government-data projects.

title: Assignment 2 – Google Trends
text:
2. Google Trends Data Using gtrendsR
Here I use the gtrendsR package and the provided script gtrendsR01.R to collect the same type of search-interest data via the API.

library(tidyverse)
library(gtrendsR)

# Run the professor's script (lightly edited to save data)
source("gtrendsR01.R")

# The script creates the_df from TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
glimpse(the_df)
head(the_df)
summary(the_df$date)

The main data frame returned by gtrendsR is interest_over_time. It contains:

date – observation date
hits – relative search interest (0–100)
keyword – search term (Trump / Harris / election)
geo – geographic region (here “US”)
gprop – type of Google search (here “web”)
category – Google Trends category (0 means no special category)

title: Assignment 2 – Google Trends
text:
4. Comparison: Website vs. gtrendsR
Google Trends Website

Very easy, point-and-click interface.
Automatically shows charts and summary statistics.
Exports a single CSV file with one column per keyword.
Good for quick, one-off exploration.

gtrendsR Package

Fully scriptable and reproducible: the code records all settings (keywords, time window, country, etc.).
Returns a tidy data frame in long format, which is easier to use with packages like dplyr and ggplot2.
Can be automated or repeated for many different queries.
Occasionally hits API limits (HTTP 429), which is a practical limitation compared to just using the website.

Overall, the website is best for quick visualization and basic download, while gtrendsR is better for systematic research where we want to re-run the same analysis or combine multiple queries.

title: Assignment 2 – Google Trends
text:
5. Conclusion
This assignment showed two complementary ways to collect data from Google Trends. The website interface makes it simple to explore search interest visually and download a ready-made CSV file. The gtrendsR package requires more setup but gives much more control over the query and produces a tidy, reproducible dataset that fits naturally into an R workflow. For a small class exercise either approach works, but for a real research project I would rely on gtrendsR so that my data collection steps are documented in code and can be updated or repeated whenever Google Trends data change.

# Top 10 counties by number of people below poverty

  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(povertyE)) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rank_group = "Highest poverty (count)")

# Bottom 10 counties by number of people below poverty

  dplyr::arrange(povertyE) |>

  dplyr::select(
    rank_group,
    county,
    povertyE, povertyM,
    med_incomeE, med_incomeM

title: Assignment 6 – Text Analytics using quanteda
text: The quanteda package is a comprehensive framework for quantitative text analysis in R. It provides tools for importing text, cleaning it, tokenizing it, and converting it into document–feature matrices (DFMs). From these DFMs, users can apply advanced text-analysis methods such as word clouds, keyness comparison, topic modeling, co-occurrence networks, and scaling models such as LSA, Wordfish, and Wordscores. Compared to base R text processing, quanteda makes it faster and more efficient to process large text collections and run reproducible analyses.

2. Biden–Xi Summit Tweets
This section uses the code in quanteda_textanalytics01.R.
The script loads tweets about the November 2021 Biden–Xi virtual summit, builds DFMs, performs latent semantic analysis (LSA), and plots hashtag and user networks.

2.1 Run the script

source("quanteda_textanalytics01.R")

2.2 Interpretation

LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis)
The LSA output shows that tweets cluster into several thematic groups. Based on the most frequent terms in each dimension, the discussions appear to revolve around:

Diplomacy & cooperation (summit, meeting, leaders, virtual talks)

Geopolitical tension (China, security, human rights, Taiwan)

U.S. domestic reactions (journalists, think-tank commentary)

These clusters reflect how Twitter conversations typically separate into news reporting, political opinion, and geopolitical analysis.


Hashtag Network Plot

textplot_network(topgat_fcm, min_freq = 50, edge_alpha = 0.8, edge_size = 1)








The hashtag network reveals groups of frequently co-occurring hashtags. For example:

News-related tags (#Breaking, #US, #China)

Political commentary tags (#Biden, #XiJinping)

Issue-specific tags (e.g., related to trade, security, diplomacy)

Hashtags that appear close together represent shared topics in the discourse.


User Mention Network Plot

textplot_network(user_fcm, min_freq = 20, edge_color = "firebrick",
                 edge_alpha = 0.8, edge_size = 1)








This network shows which accounts dominate the conversation. Central users typically include:

Journalists reporting on the summit

News outlets

Political commentators

Analysts covering U.S.–China relations

The high degree of clustering indicates that a small number of influential accounts shape much of the discussion.

title: Assignment 6 – Text Analytics using quanteda
text:
3. U.S. Presidential Inaugural Speeches
This section uses the code in quanteda_textanalytics02.R.
The script analyzes the U.S. inaugural address corpus using wordclouds, keyword-in-context (KWIC), frequency charts, and text scaling.

3.1 Run the script

source("quanteda_textanalytics02.R")
























3.2 Interpretation

Early Inaugural Speech Wordclouds
The earliest speeches (1789–1826) emphasize terms such as government, duty, public, union, and people.
This reflects the period’s preoccupation with defining governmental roles and stabilizing the new republic.


Comparing Bush, Obama, and Trump Wordclouds
The comparison wordcloud shows clear stylistic differences:

Bush: terms relating to security, freedom, resolve

Obama: focus on hope, unity, responsibility

Trump: “America-first” framing, strong emphasis on national identity

These terms highlight ideological and rhetorical distinctions between administrations.


KWIC + X-Ray Plots
KWIC searches for words such as “american”, “people”, and “communist” reveal how each term’s use varies by president.
The x-ray plot shows that:

“American” appears more frequently in later decades

“People” remains a consistently common term

“Communist” spikes during Cold War speeches



Frequency Plot for “american”
This plot shows the rising use of the term “american” over time.
It suggests a growing rhetorical emphasis on national identity throughout the 20th and 21st centuries.


Keyness Analysis: Trump vs. Obama
Keyness identifies words most strongly associated with one president versus the other.

Words with positive keyness → more common in Trump’s speech

Words with negative keyness → more common in Obama’s speech

This captures stylistic and thematic contrasts between the two presidents.

title: Assignment 6 – Text Analytics using quanteda
text:
4. What is Wordfish?
Wordfish is an unsupervised text scaling model that estimates:

A latent dimension (e.g., ideology)
Word discrimination values
Document positions on the latent scale

It uses a Poisson model of word counts:

Words that strongly indicate one side of the scale receive high discrimination values

Documents containing those words more frequently get shifted toward that side of the latent dimension

The model is often used to measure:

Party ideology

Policy stance

Rhetorical positioning

In this assignment’s script, Wordfish is demonstrated using Irish budget speeches, showing how parties and years align on an inferred economic policy dimension.

text: Druckrey uses thin and thick lines, as well as curves and straight lines, to teach students to recognize subtle differences in visual weight and movement. Her exercises require students to repeatedly draw lines while controlling pressure, spacing, length, and alignment. A line is therefore not simply a geometric object; its thickness and rhythm can change how the eye experiences a composition. Similarly, curves introduce movement and organic qualities that cannot always be captured by rigid geometric construction. These exercises train the eye and hand to work together and help students understand visual relationships before worrying about the meaning or content of a design

title: Assignment 1
section: 2. Holmes on the eye and hand in writing
text:
2. Holmes on the eye and hand in writing
Kris Holmes describes a tension between the eye and the hand. The eye tends to be conservative, seeking order, regularity, consistency, and rhythm. The hand is more radical, naturally producing movement, variation, and individual expression. Writing therefore contains a record of physical movement: even when letters are transformed into standardized typefaces, traces of the hand remain important to how letterforms are perceived. This explains why typography requires a balance between structure and organic expression rather than being purely mechanical.

title: Assignment 1
section: 3. Calligraphy, Steve Jobs, and the Macintosh
text:
3. Calligraphy, Steve Jobs, and the Macintosh
Calligraphy was important to Steve Jobs because it introduced him to the artistic and historical qualities of letterforms, including serif and sans-serif typefaces, spacing between letters, and typography. While studying at Reed College, Jobs initially saw calligraphy as having no practical application. Years later, however, he recognized its influence while designing the Macintosh. He credited his calligraphy experience with inspiring the Mac’s multiple typefaces and proportionally spaced fonts, helping make typography an integral part of the computer’s design rather than merely functional text.

title: Assignment 1
text:
4. Geometric versus optical accuracy
The film makes an important distinction between geometric accuracy and optical accuracy. Geometric accuracy means that something is mathematically or physically equal—for example, two letters may have exactly the same measured weight or two spaces may have identical dimensions. Optical accuracy asks whether they look equal to the human eye. Druckrey demonstrates that these are not always the same. Two letters with identical measurements can appear to have different visual weights, and equal measured spaces can appear uneven. Therefore, designers sometimes have to deliberately violate mathematical precision to achieve visual balance.
Overall, Teaching to See emphasizes that design is not simply about following rules or making mathematically precise forms. It is about developing the ability to see deeply, understand visual relationships, and use both disciplined observation and expressive movement. Druckrey’s teaching shows that the most successful designs emerge when measurement, perception, and the human hand work together.

title: Assignment 1
text: Anugraha’s Data Guide

title: Assignment 1
text:
1. Source and Provenance
Before working with the data, I need to understand how it came into existence.

Who created or collected the data? Is the original source identifiable?
How were the data collected? Was the information obtained through surveys, administrative records, sensors, observations, manual entry, or another method?
Am I working with the original data or a modified version? If another person or organisation processed the data, do I know what was changed?
Is the methodology documented clearly enough for me to understand the dataset’s limitations?
Could the source have incentives, procedures, or collection constraints that systematically influence what appears in the data?
2. Completeness and Missing Data

Missing information can change the meaning of an analysis, so I should understand absence before treating it as insignificant.

Are values missing? If so, do I know what the missing values mean?
Are zeros, blanks, negative values, or unusual codes being used as substitutes for missing information?
Are records missing that I would reasonably expect to be present, such as particular years, geographic areas, groups, or categories?
Is the dataset complete for the time period, population, and geographic area I intend to discuss?
Could missing observations systematically affect the pattern or conclusion I see?
3. Structure, Definitions, and Consistency

Before calculating anything, I should determine whether the dataset is internally consistent.

Are any rows, observations, or identifiers duplicated?
Are categories, names, locations, and labels spelled and coded consistently?
Are dates stored and interpreted consistently?
Are units clearly defined? For example, do I know whether a value represents dollars, percentages, people, rates, kilograms, miles, or another unit?
Are variable and column names clear enough that I understand what each field actually measures?
Are identifiers such as ZIP codes, FIPS codes, IDs, or account numbers being treated as identifiers rather than meaningful numerical quantities?
4. Plausibility and Data Quality

I should perform basic reality checks rather than assuming unusual values are valid.

What are the minimum, maximum, average, and general distribution of important variables?
Are any values impossible, implausible, or unexpectedly extreme?
Are there unexplained outliers that could represent errors, unusual cases, or important phenomena?
Do I see suspicious placeholder values, such as repeated 9s, repeated zeros, unusual default dates, or other codes that may not represent real observations?
Does the level of numerical precision make sense for the way the variable was actually measured?
If published totals or summaries are available, do my calculations agree with them?
5. Sampling, Measurement, and Representation

A clean dataset can still produce misleading conclusions if it does not adequately represent the population or concept being studied.

What population does this dataset actually represent?
How were cases or participants selected? Was the sample random, convenience-based, voluntary, or produced through another process?
Could certain groups be systematically underrepresented or overrepresented?
If the data come from a sample or survey, is uncertainty such as a margin of error available and reasonable?
Do the variables actually measure the concepts I want to discuss, or am I using a convenient proxy?
Does the evidence support the conclusion I want to make, or would my interpretation go beyond what the data can establish?
6. Time, Geography, and Aggregation

Patterns can change depending on when, where, and at what level data are grouped.

Are the time periods I am comparing genuinely comparable?
Could seasonal patterns or other natural variation explain an apparent increase or decrease?
If financial values are compared across time, do I need to account for inflation or changing monetary value?
Is the geographic level appropriate for my question, or are the data too broad or too detailed?
Could aggregation hide meaningful differences among neighborhoods, demographic groups, organizations, or other subgroups?
Am I comparing categories, locations, or time periods that were defined or measured in the same way?
7. Before Visualization and Communication

A technically correct calculation can still produce a misleading visualization. Before publishing or presenting my work, I will check whether the visual representation accurately reflects the strength and limitations of the evidence.

Have I preserved the original data and documented important cleaning or transformation decisions?
Could missing data materially change the pattern shown in the visualization?
Does my visualization imply greater certainty or precision than the data support?
Could my choice of scale, categories, aggregation, or time frame exaggerate or conceal an important pattern?
Have I represented uncertainty where it is important to interpretation?
Can I clearly explain where the data came from, what each major variable represents, and how I transformed the data?
Would another person have enough information to reproduce the important steps of my analysis?
Have I disclosed limitations that could materially affect how the audience should interpret the visualization?

ABOUT ME





I am a graduate student in Social Data Analytics at The University of Texas at Dallas, with an academic background in Psychology and Sociology.
My interests sit at the intersection of people, data, and society. I am particularly interested in using quantitative and computational methods to better understand human behavior, social patterns, and the ways in which data can be communicated clearly and responsibly.

title: About
text:
My Background
My academic training in psychology and sociology shaped the way I approach data.
Rather than viewing data simply as numbers, I am interested in the people, behaviors, institutions, and social processes represented behind those numbers.
My current graduate studies in Social Data Analytics allow me to combine this social-science perspective with computational methods, statistical analysis, and data visualization.
Through my coursework, I have been developing experience working with different forms of social data and learning how analytical and visual methods can be used to identify patterns, communicate evidence, and support thoughtful interpretation.

title: About
text:
What I’m Interested In


Social Data
I am interested in using data to understand social behavior, demographic patterns, inequality, public opinion, and other questions related to society and human behavior.


Data Visualization
I am interested in how design choices influence what people notice, understand, and conclude from data.
For me, visualization is not simply about producing attractive charts. It is a way of organizing evidence and making complex information easier to interpret.


Human-Centered Research
My background in psychology and sociology has made me particularly interested in research that focuses on people’s experiences, behaviors, and decision-making.
This includes areas such as user research, survey research, and mixed-method approaches.

title: About
text:
Methods & Tools
My coursework and projects involve a growing set of analytical and visualization methods.

R ggplot2 Data Visualization Statistical Analysis Social Data Analysis Survey Research Spatial Data Text Analysis Data Cleaning Research Design

title: About
text:
Current Focus
I am currently focused on strengthening my ability to move from a research question to a clear and defensible analysis.
That means thinking carefully about:

what question the data can actually answer,
how data should be collected and prepared,
which visual representation best fits the evidence,
how design affects interpretation,
and what limitations should be acknowledged when drawing conclusions.

This portfolio documents that learning process through coursework and independent exploration.

title: About
text:
Beyond the Classroom
I am continuing to explore how social-science research, data analytics, visualization, and human-centered research can come together in professional practice.
I am especially interested in projects that require both analytical reasoning and an understanding of people — where quantitative evidence can be combined with thoughtful interpretation to help answer meaningful questions.
